summary.text: Reflection is a wave bouncing back into the medium it came from when it meets the boundary with a different medium.
At a mirror-like surface, the angle a wave arrives at equals the angle it leaves at, both measured from the line perpendicular to the surface.
It works for light, sound, water waves and radio, and it explains echoes, sonar, radar and the images that mirrors form.

facts.label: Law of reflection
facts.value: θᵢ = θ_r: incidence angle equals reflection angle

facts.label: Two kinds
facts.value: Specular reflection keeps the image; diffuse reflection loses it

facts.label: Making a mirror
facts.value: A glass sheet with a metallic coating

facts.label: Beyond light
facts.value: Even X-rays and gamma rays reflect at shallow angles

facts.label: Phase flip
facts.value: Reflecting off higher-index material shifts the wave 180 degrees

items.prompt: A flashlight beam strikes a bathroom mirror at a slant. How does the beam leave the mirror?

options.label: At a steeper angle, since the mirror pushes it back
Straight back along the line it arrived on
At the same angle it arrived, measured from the perpendicular
At a shallower angle, since the mirror soaks up some

items.explain: For mirror-like reflection the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (θᵢ = θ_r), and the two rays sit on opposite sides of the perpendicular.

items.prompt: You can see your face in a mirror but not in a matte painted wall, though both send light back. What is the difference?

options.label: The wall swallows the light and the mirror returns it
The wall scatters the light, keeping its energy but losing the image
The mirror speeds the light up so the image stays sharp
The wall only reflects sound while the mirror reflects light

items.explain: Diffuse reflection keeps the energy but loses the image, while mirror-like (specular) reflection preserves the image.

items.prompt: A fishing boat sends sound pulses into the water and listens for what returns to locate a school of fish. Which effect does this rely on?

options.label: Sound curving around the fish as it passes
Sound turning into light when it hits something
Sound slowing down in the fish and stopping
Sound bouncing off objects and coming back

items.explain: Reflection of sound causes echoes and is the principle behind sonar.

items.prompt: Astronomers want to focus X-rays, but an ordinary mirror would just let them pass through. How do X-ray telescopes handle this?

options.label: They let the waves skim a funnel-shaped surface at a low angle
They coat a flat mirror with a much thicker layer of metal
They slow the X-rays down first until a mirror can catch them
They aim the waves straight at a curved surface head-on

items.explain: The waves hit a converging tunnel at a low angle and reflect toward the focus, whereas a conventional reflector would be useless.

items.prompt: Light hits a clear window pane. Some of it passes through. What happens to the rest?

options.label: None bounces off, since glass is transparent
All of it is absorbed by the glass as heat
A fraction reflects at the surface, though less than a mirror would
It all reflects, and the see-through part is an illusion

items.explain: Reflection also happens at transparent surfaces like glass, where a fraction is reflected and the remainder is refracted.

items.prompt: Hold up a page of writing to a mirror and the words look flipped left to right. Why does the image seem reversed?

options.label: The mirror swaps left and right sides on purpose
We compare it with what we would see if we turned into its position
Light reverses its direction of travel inside the glass
The metallic coating flips the writing as it reflects

items.explain: A flat surface forms a mirror image that only appears reversed because we compare it with what we would see after rotating into the image's position.

paragraphs.heading: Bouncing back
paragraphs.text: Reflection happens when a wave meets the boundary between two different materials and turns back into the material it came from. Light, sound and water waves all do it. In sound, reflection gives us echoes and makes sonar work. Geologists rely on it when they study seismic waves.

paragraphs.heading: The law of reflection
paragraphs.text: At a mirror-like surface, a wave leaves at the same angle it arrived at. To measure those angles, imagine a line standing straight out from the surface at the point where the ray hits; this line is called the normal. The law then says θᵢ = θ_r: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. The incoming ray, the outgoing ray and the normal all sit in one flat plane, with the two rays on opposite sides of the normal.

paragraphs.heading: Mirror-like or scattered
paragraphs.text: Reflected light can be specular, meaning mirror-like, or diffuse, where the energy comes back but the image is lost. Which one you get depends on the kind of surface. A typical mirror is a sheet of glass with a metal coating, and the coating does most of the reflecting. Clear materials such as water and glass reflect too, but usually less well than a mirror.

paragraphs.heading: Images in mirrors
paragraphs.text: Specular reflection makes images. A flat mirror gives a mirror image that seems swapped left to right, because we judge it against how we would look if we were turned around to stand where the image is. A curved mirror can make an image larger or smaller, and such mirrors may be spherical or parabolic in shape.

paragraphs.heading: Part reflected, part passed on
paragraphs.text: Light can reflect any time it crosses from one material into another with a different refractive index. Usually some of the light reflects at the boundary and the rest carries on and bends, which is called refraction. Equations called the Fresnel equations predict how the light splits between the two. When light reflects off a material with a higher refractive index than the one it is in, its wave is flipped by 180°, an effect that matters in thin-film optics.

paragraphs.heading: Why materials reflect
paragraphs.text: In classical physics, light is an electromagnetic wave. When it hits a material, it makes the atoms, or the electrons in a metal, jiggle slightly, and each one sends out a small wave of its own in every direction. These little waves add up to produce both reflection and refraction. In glass, the reflected light is the sum of the backward-going waves from all the electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Reflecting X-rays
paragraphs.text: Reflection is not limited to visible light. Radio waves of VHF and higher frequencies reflect, which matters for radio and radar. Special grazing mirrors can bounce even hard X-rays and gamma rays, as long as the rays come in at a shallow angle. X-ray telescopes use a narrowing tunnel whose walls send the rays at low angles toward a detector at the focus, because an ordinary mirror would just let the X-rays pass through.
